terms.gloss: let fly, discharge (a missile); let go
throw about, keep throwing, toss around
evidence: Ov. Tr. 4.2.50: jactātō flōre tegente viās (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: The frequentative of jaciō: throwing things about again and again, which is what a child is told not to do.

phrases.latin: pater eam lēniter conjiciēbat, Theodōrus manibus excipiēbat, aut, sī ēlāpsa erat, pede ad patrem pulsābat
phrases.english: Dad tossed it gently, Theo caught it in his hands or, if it slipped, kicked it back to Dad

phrases.latin: Ibi follem, quem puerī quīdam pede pulsābant, ad sē volūtum Theodōrus ambābus manibus ad eōs conjēcit.
phrases.english: There some boys were kicking a ball; when it rolled to him Theo threw it back to them with both hands.
phrases.source: Libellus V, Lisbōna: castellum et ōceanārium

phrases.english: Don’t throw your toys about; they’ll break.

phrases.latin: Nōlī quicquam jacere intus; forīs pilā lūdēmus.
phrases.english: Don’t throw anything indoors; we’ll play ball outside.
Throw a pebble into the water.
Don’t throw stones at the birds.

phrases.latin: Deucaliōn vacuum lapidēs jactāvit in orbem
phrases.english: Deucalion threw stones into the empty world

sources: Lewis & Short: conicio · Lewis & Short: emitto · Lewis & Short: jacto
John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency, p. 44.

Theodōrus et pater · Ad Larem avītum, Libellī I–VII, as they stood on 7 November 2026, with their glosses. Examples marked “Libellus” quote those texts word for word; classical passages are cited by author.
